summary: Monkey, Pigsy, and Sandy guard the monk Tripitaka on a comic, demon-haunted pilgrimage to India for Buddhist scriptures, fighting monsters that want to eat him.

hunger.why: Pigsy's bottomless appetite, the pilgrims begging for meals, Monkey gorging on the peaches of immortality, and demons craving Tripitaka's flesh keep food in view.

thirst.why: The pilgrims drink from the river of the Women's Kingdom and become pregnant; otherwise water is rarely an issue.

feeling-cold-hot.why: The Flaming Mountain blocks the road with unbearable heat until Monkey wins the palm-leaf fan.

sleepiness.why: Pigsy dozes when sent to scout and the pilgrims are often weary, a minor comic note.

curiosity.why: Every chapter brings a new kingdom, mountain, or cave, and Monkey scouts each unfamiliar land ahead of the party.

explanation-seeking.why: Monkey sees through disguised demons such as the White Bone Spirit and uncovers the false king of the Black Rooster Kingdom.

skill-acquisition.why: Monkey learns immortality, the seventy-two transformations, and the cloud somersault from Subhuti before the journey begins.

play.why: Monkey's mischief in Heaven and his pranks on Pigsy are playful, and the Monkey King's early rule is a kind of game.

resource-accumulation.why: Monkey takes the golden staff and armor from the Dragon King and seizes demons' magic gourds and treasures.

resource-foraging.why: The quest itself is a search for the scriptures, and episodes turn on finding the fan, water, or food in hostile lands.

mental-time-travel.why: Monkey devises stratagems against each demon, and the pilgrims are told their journey will take eighty-one ordeals.

fear-of-predators.why: Demon after demon, from the White Bone Spirit to the spider women, tries to capture and eat Tripitaka to gain immortality.

fear-of-aggressors.why: Monkey battles Heaven's armies, and the pilgrims fight demon hosts and hostile kings throughout.

fear-of-heights.why: Monkey somersaults through the clouds and the party crosses mountains, but falls are not feared.

disgust.why: Demon lairs strewn with bones, the Women's Kingdom pregnancies, and Pigsy's filth add occasional grossness.

pain-aversion.why: Tripitaka tightens the headband spell to torment Monkey, and the fights leave wounds; suffering is real but comic.

pride.why: Monkey proclaims himself Great Sage Equal to Heaven and glories in beating every rival.

shame.why: Monkey weeps when Tripitaka dismisses him, and Pigsy is repeatedly caught in disgrace.

moral-pride.why: Tripitaka refuses to harm any being even when it endangers him, and Monkey's loyalty to his master holds despite mistreatment.

guilt.why: Monkey shows little remorse for his rebellion; guilt is rare in the novel.

warmth.why: Guanyin's mercy and Tripitaka's kindness to strangers recur, even when misplaced.

moral-blame.why: Tripitaka condemns Monkey for killing the disguised White Bone Spirit, and the pilgrims expose corrupt kings and false monks.

moral-praise.why: The pilgrims are rewarded with Buddhahood for completing the journey, and kingdoms thank them for ridding them of demons.

revenge.why: Red Boy's kin and the Bull Demon King seek to repay Monkey, and Monkey settles old scores from his rebellion.

forgiveness.why: Tripitaka takes Monkey back after each dismissal, and Buddha's mercy ends Monkey's punishment under the mountain.

compassion.why: Tripitaka pities every creature, and the pilgrims rescue villages, children, and prisoners from demons.

affiliation.why: Tripitaka gathers Monkey, Pigsy, Sandy, and the dragon horse as companions in the early chapters.

friendship.why: The bickering fellowship of Monkey, Pigsy, and Sandy, loyal through eighty-one ordeals, carries the book.

sadness.why: Grief is brief and quickly overturned; Monkey's tears at dismissal are the main instance.

humor.why: Pigsy's gluttony and lechery, Monkey's tricks, and the constant squabbling make the novel a comedy.

embarrassment.why: Pigsy is exposed in his lust when the bodhisattvas test him and is left tied in the trees.

reasoning.why: Monkey talks his way past demons and argues with Heaven's officials, but debate is incidental.

coalitional-affiliation.why: The pilgrim band and the celestial hierarchy form groups, and demons often ally against the party.

status-seeking.why: Monkey rebels because Heaven makes him a stable boy and demands the title Great Sage Equal to Heaven.

envy.why: Monkey resents the immortals' privileges, but envy is not sustained.

anger.why: Monkey's rage against Heaven and against demons, and Tripitaka's anger at Monkey, fuel many episodes.

hatred.why: Monkey enjoys the downfall of demons, but gloating is minor.

romantic-affiliation.why: Pigsy's marriage at Gao village and the queen of the Women's Kingdom wanting to wed Tripitaka are comic episodes.

sexual-attraction.why: Pigsy lusts after every woman, and female demons use beauty to seduce the pilgrims.

long-term-love.why: The Bull Demon King and Princess Iron Fan are a married couple, but committed love is incidental.

desire.why: Pigsy's lechery is a running joke, from his fall from Heaven for harassing the Moon Goddess onward.

romantic-jealousy.why: Princess Iron Fan resents the Bull Demon King's concubine, a brief episode.

sexual-jealousy.why: The same marital quarrel over the Jade-Faced Fox is the only instance.

sexual-disgust.why: The scorpion demon and other she-monsters try to force Tripitaka into their beds, which he resists with horror.

parental-care.why: Red Boy's parents fight for him and the pilgrims rescue children offered to demons.

parental-investment.why: Subhuti and then Tripitaka teach and discipline Monkey as a master does a disciple, a parental echo at most.

familial-love.why: The Bull Demon King's family and Tripitaka's recovered parents appear, but family bonds are marginal.
